svg.text: Breaking bad news, and the family who ask you not to
The commonest ethical knot on a Ghanaian ward: relatives who love the patient asking you to keep the truth from her.
A structure that works
Find a private place and sit down.
Ask what she already understands.
Ask how much she wants to know.
Give a warning, then the news, in plain words.
Stop talking. Let the silence do its work.
Respond to the feeling before the facts.
Agree what happens next, and say you will return.
Most of it is asking and waiting, not telling.
"Doctor, please do not tell her"
Do not agree, and do not overrule them either.
Ask what they are afraid will happen if she
is told. The fear is usually that she will give up,
or that they will have to watch her suffer.
Then explain that you will not lie to her, and
that you will not force information on her.
You will follow her own questions. Most families
accept this, because it answers what they feared.
Care that continues when treatment stops
A decision not to attempt resuscitation is a decision about one intervention only. Pain relief, mouth care, positioning,
company and honest answers all continue, and usually intensify. Nothing about that decision means less nursing.
Never write or say that there is nothing more to be done.
After the death, in a Ghanaian setting
Loud, public, communal grieving is normal and healthy here, not a breakdown to be sedated or hushed. Give the family
a private space and time with the body, ask about washing and religious rites before you proceed, and explain the
mortuary and documentation steps once, slowly, then write them down because nobody remembers them.
